findings.title: Delete routing contradicts the prescribed collision-remediation path — `cf config unset --project` cannot clear the stale shared-file copy, and following the prescription destroys the personal value
findings.description: The Data Flow states delete "mirrors write — deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to," and explicitly names `migrate-personal` as "the one exception that touches the *other* project file." For a personal key, that means `cf config unset <key> --project` deletes only from `.context-forge.local.toml`. But the Collision semantics paragraph (`:146`) prescribes clearing the stale *shared-file* copy via "a separate, explicit `cf config unset <key> --project` the user can run once they've confirmed the personal value is correct," and Verification Walkthrough step 9 (`:259`) instructs the same, expecting "`cf check` is clean again." Under the design's own Delete semantics this is impossible: unset removes the developer's *personal* value (the exact data loss the design says it must prevent), the stale shared copy survives, the read falls back to it, and the checker finding persists — so walkthrough step 9 cannot pass and the prescribed user path actively harms the user. The design must pick and state one resolution before the collision-handling work is implemented, e.g.: `delete` on a personal key also removes any shared-file copy (which is stale by definition once flagged), or `migrate-personal` gains an explicit way to clear the divergent shared copy.

findings.title: No specified home for the new cross-file config operations — `ConfigManager`'s TOML helpers are module-private, so the component map implies duplicated TOML key-walking or undocumented core exports
findings.description: Two new consumers need file-level capabilities the `ConfigManager` public API does not provide: (a) `migrate-personal`, placed in `packages/cli/src/commands/config.ts` (`:65`), must enumerate personal keys present in the shared file and move keys between the two files; (b) the new `ConsistencyChecker` rule (`:142`) must scan the shared file for present personal keys. `readToml`/`writeToml`/`resolveKey`/`setKey`/`deleteKey` are non-exported module functions inside `ConfigManager.ts`, and the design's export list for `packages/core/src/config/index.ts` mentions only the new path helper — so an implementer following the component map literally must either re-implement dotted-key TOML manipulation in the CLI and in `introspection` (violating the project's DRY and "program to interfaces" conventions) or invent a core export the design never names. The design should specify the migration/scan logic's home (e.g., a `ConfigManager.migratePersonalKeys()` method or exported file-level helpers in `core/config`) so the layering and DRY rules are decidable rather than left to implementation.

findings.title: `config_get` MCP tool description will misstate the resolution order after the precedence change; the design's `configTools.ts` update omits the description string
findings.description: Technical Scope commits to updating `packages/mcp-server/src/tools/configTools.ts` to surface both project paths, but the current `config_get` description string reads "Resolution order: project config → user config → built-in default," which becomes incorrect for personal keys under the new project-personal → project-shared → user → default precedence. For an MCP tool whose primary consumer is an LLM agent, the description is the interface contract agents reason from; the design should include the one-line description update (and note that `config_set`'s scope wording remains accurate) as part of the `configTools.ts` change it already scopes.

findings.title: `migrate-personal`'s `--project <id>` flag form diverges from the sibling config subcommands' optional-value convention
findings.description: The API contract shows `cf config migrate-personal [-p, --project <id>]` (required-value form), while `config get`/`set`/`unset` all declare `-p, --project [id]` where a bare flag resolves from CWD. The walkthrough also always passes an explicit `<id>`. Aligning with the `[id]` optional-value convention (and the 907 centralized `withProjectOption`) would make the new subcommand consistent with the command family it joins; not blocking.

findings.title: Verification walkthrough presumes `.gitignore` handling runs under `cf init --lite`, but the design doesn't pin where in `init.ts` the gitignore step lands
findings.description: The `.gitignore` handling section correctly confirms no gitignore-writing logic exists today, but the walkthrough (step 1) uses `cf init --lite` and then expects `.context-forge.local.toml` in `.gitignore` (step 3), while `init.ts` skips its entire setup block (`if (!opts.lite)`) for guides/commands/IDE. The design should state that the gitignore append runs unconditionally (outside the lite gate, alongside project registration) so the walkthrough passes as written for both init modes.

findings.title: Design declares `dependencies: [914]` where the plan entry lists "Dependencies: none"
findings.description: The added dependency is justified in the Prerequisites section (the canonical personal key must already carry its final `git.integration_branch` name) and is already satisfied (914 is complete), so there is no functional impact — but it is a metadata divergence from the slice plan entry worth recording for traceability.

findings.title: Migration/compat story fully satisfies the plan's requirement and the design's codebase claims verify under inspection
findings.description: The plan entry demands "a defined migration/compat story for projects that already committed personal keys"; the design delivers a complete one — read-time fallback preserving current behavior (verified consistent with the existing `readToml` ENOENT→empty and precedence-chain patterns in `ConfigManager.ts`), warning-severity detection via `ConsistencyChecker` (`'warning'` is a valid `ConsistencySeverity`), and an idempotent `migrate-personal` command with write-personal-then-delete-shared ordering, per-key failure isolation, and explicit no-overwrite collision semantics. The rejection of an auto-fix path is correct: `ConsistencyFinding.fixAction.type` is confirmed as the closed `'update-checkbox' | 'update-frontmatter'` union in `packages/core/src/introspection/types.ts`, and the design's claim that both `cf check` and MCP `workflow_check` run the full checker suite (so the new rule surfaces without touching either command file) matches the actual construction sites in `check.ts` and `workflowTools.ts`. Factual claims about `ConfigResult.source` consumers (`config.ts:86,100` template interpolation, MCP pass-through with no exhaustive switch) and about zero existing gitignore-writing logic also verify.
